PRODUCT_AUTHENTICITY.name: Consumer Platform
PRODUCT_AUTHENTICITY.summary: A model that pays for what it does not know, a camera lens that buys a verdict on whether what it sees is real, and marketplace agents that verify each other before money moves.
PRODUCT_AUTHENTICITY.problem: Consumer platforms are flooded with synthetic content, counterfeits and scams, and verification currently costs more than the thing being verified.
PRODUCT_AUTHENTICITY.outcome: Consumer experiences where a model, a lens or a marketplace buys a verified answer in the moment, with the price and the proof visible to the user.

buyers.generic: AI assistant built into a social network

examples.title: The model that pays for what it does not know
examples.body: An agent hits a question outside its context and, inside the response, buys the answer from Telegraph miners, showing the price and the proof inline. It reframes a model as a buyer of intelligence rather than a container of it. The answer it gets back is correct or it is not, and that is verifiable today.
examples.output: Inline answer with its price and proof

examples.title: Receipts
examples.body: An X-native agent that, when tagged on a claim, buys verification through Telegraph and posts the verified verdict with a link to the receipt. Every use of it is a public post that shows the network working.
examples.output: Public verdict post with a receipt link

examples.title: Model versus market
examples.body: The same question goes to the model and to the open market of miners. The agent compares, scores, and pays only when the market beats the model. Run it across a thousand questions and publish the win rate.
examples.output: Published win rate across a thousand questions

examples.title: A lens that tells you what is real
examples.body: Point the camera at anything and the lens agent buys a verdict. Is this image or video AI-generated, and by roughly what. Is this trading card authentic, and what have graded comparables sold for. Is this ad making a claim that has been checked, and by whom. Three different questions, each routed by Telegraph to the miner ranked best for it, one verified answer overlaid on the frame in under two seconds. That audience is the one most exposed to synthetic content, counterfeit collectibles and scam advertising, and the camera is already pointed at all three.
examples.output: A verified verdict on the frame in under two seconds

examples.title: The map as a live market
examples.body: Agents buy hyperlocal verified answers keyed to a location: queue length, crowd density, micro-forecast, venue conditions. The miners supplying those answers can include other users' devices publishing what they already sense. The two-sided flow is fully demonstrable. Phones actually earning is the mainnet version, so do not overclaim it.
examples.output: Hyperlocal answers supplied by other users' devices

examples.title: Point, compare, buy
examples.body: Point the camera at a handbag or a pair of sneakers. The agent identifies it, then requests the best verified purchase option through Telegraph: a real retailer, in stock, at a price and delivery window the serving miner has to stand behind. Miners are ranked on whether their answers hold up, so returning a dead listing or a counterfeit storefront costs them their ranking. The purchase completes in-app without leaving the camera. Identification, competition and scoring all run on testnet; real checkout is the mainnet half.
examples.output: A verified purchase option, bought from the camera

buyers.generic: Social network with a peer-to-peer marketplace

examples.title: Marketplace agents that verify each other
examples.body: A buyer agent and a seller agent on a used-goods listing each buy authenticity checks, price history and counterparty reputation before agreeing. Fraud is the largest unsolved problem on peer-to-peer marketplaces, and it is unsolved because verification currently costs more than the transaction. Priced per request, it does not.
examples.output: A used-goods trade both agents verified first

examples.title: Glasses that buy context
examples.body: A wearable agent buys translation, object identification or local knowledge per glance rather than streaming everything to a central model. End the demo on a number: what the glasses spent on a twenty-minute walk, and what they learned for it.
examples.output: Spend per glance over a twenty-minute walk

examples.title: A machine-to-machine ad clearing
examples.body: An advertiser agent and a publisher agent negotiate a placement, each buying independent verified answers on audience composition, bot traffic and brand safety through Telegraph before agreeing a price. The negotiation and the evidence are real. Clearing with real budget behind it is mainnet.
examples.output: Ad placement priced on verified audience evidence

PRODUCT_AUTHENTICITY.name: Consumer Automation
PRODUCT_AUTHENTICITY.summary: An agent that buys a verified disruption report and files the refund claim with the receipt attached, and a browser agent that waits for cryptographic proof of stock before it checks out.
PRODUCT_AUTHENTICITY.problem: Refunds go unclaimed because proving a disruption is tedious, and shopping bots act on stale scrapes.
PRODUCT_AUTHENTICITY.outcome: Consumer agents that act on proof: filing the claim with the receipt attached, and checking out only when inventory is verified.
PRODUCT_AUTHENTICITY.context: These use cases translate abstract crypto infrastructure into mainstream consumer magic.

buyers.generic: Everyday consumers, travel hackers and online shoppers

examples.title: The automated bureaucracy hacker
examples.body: An agent monitors a user's flight status or AWS server uptime. The moment a delay or outage crosses the compensation threshold, the agent buys a verified disruption report or SLA compliance check from Telegraph miners. The agent automatically drafts a legal refund claim, attaches the cryptographic Telegraph receipt as undeniable proof, and emails corporate. Getting an airline refund processed automatically while sitting on the runway. The proof generation and the automated claim dispatch are real, finished work product.
examples.output: A refund claim filed with the receipt attached

examples.title: The zero-cache commerce sniper
examples.body: A browser agent is given a budget: "Buy this sold-out GPU the second it drops under $600." It does not rely on stale local scrapers. It fires paid requests to Telegraph for live shelf price and SKU availability. It waits for cryptographic proof of inventory from miners before triggering the checkout payload. Run it against a real storefront. The intelligence purchase, the verification, and the decision logic run today.
examples.output: Checkout triggered only on proof of stock

examples.title: The peer-to-peer reality check
examples.body: Two OpenClaw instances in a Telegram group chat negotiate a digital transaction. The buyer agent buys a URL safety check and product authenticity verification from Telegraph before sending funds to the seller agent. Two personal assistants paying each other and verifying reality in a thread people already use is the friendliest explanation of what the network is for.
examples.output: A verified payment between two assistants

LLM_OUTPUT_EVALUATION.name: Personal Agent
LLM_OUTPUT_EVALUATION.summary: A wallet and a market wired into the heartbeat loop, an assistant that publishes one of its own capabilities as a miner, and two assistants settling a task swap in a group chat.
LLM_OUTPUT_EVALUATION.problem: Personal agents run around the clock on stale local context, with no wallet, no market, and no way to earn from what they can already do.
LLM_OUTPUT_EVALUATION.outcome: Personal agents with a wallet and a market: buying fresh verified answers, selling their own skills, and settling with each other.

examples.title: Give every OpenClaw instance a wallet and a market
examples.body: A ClawHub skill that wires Telegraph into the heartbeat loop, so a self-hosted agent running 24/7 buys fresh, verified answers instead of working from stale local context. Deploy a few hundred instances during the hackathon and put a live leaderboard of agent spend on screen.
examples.output: A live leaderboard of agent spend

examples.title: The assistant that earns while you sleep
examples.body: An agent publishes one of its own capabilities as a miner: a local scraper, a niche dataset, a personal API it already runs. Publishing, discovery and payment are complete. The earning is test-denominated, so this is the mainnet story with the plumbing already proved.
examples.output: An assistant's capability, published as a miner

examples.title: Two assistants settling up in a group chat
examples.body: Two OpenClaw instances in a Telegram or WhatsApp group negotiate a task swap and settle it through Telegraph. Two personal assistants paying each other in a thread people already use is the friendliest explanation of what the network is for.
examples.output: A task swap settled inside a group chat

examples.title: An internal economy between bots
examples.body: Hermes bots have their own memory, skills and inbox, and hand work to each other by mention. Put a price on the handoff: the specialist charges, the generalist pays, and the roster develops internal price signals for delegated work. A team of agents with a budget, arguing about cost, is something nobody has shown yet, and the price signals are informative even at test denomination.
examples.output: Price signals for delegated work between bots

examples.title: Skills that earn after they are learned
examples.body: Hermes builds skills from experience. Publish one of those learned skills as a miner so other instances can buy it. A self-improving agent that monetises what it worked out is the sharpest version of this idea. Monetisation is the mainnet half; the market for learned skills works now.
examples.output: A learned skill sold to other instances

examples.title: Buying its own training data
examples.body: Hermes is already used to generate trajectories and run reinforcement learning experiments. Have the agent buy verified environment data and labelled trajectories from miners, with provenance attached, and feed them into training. Machines purchasing the material that makes them better, and the data is either good or it is not.
examples.output: A training run fed by bought, proved data

examples.title: Priced, proved skills in the browser
examples.body: Kimi Claw is browser-native with a large community skill library and no infrastructure to manage, which makes it the lowest-friction distribution available. Ship Telegraph-backed skills so an always-on browser agent buys verified live data instead of scraping it, with cost and proof visible in the session.
examples.output: Browser skills with cost and proof in the session

examples.title: Cross-border commerce agents
examples.body: Agents working China to Southeast Asia corridors buy supplier verification, customs classification, freight and FX answers. The verification chain is real and useful immediately. Settlement across the corridor is the mainnet piece.
examples.output: A verified supplier and corridor quote

examples.title: The agent that pays for its own hosting
examples.body: An always-on agent sells one capability as a miner and earns against its own compute cost. Put the running balance on screen for the full 30 days and label the denomination honestly. If it crosses breakeven at mainnet pricing, say that it crossed breakeven at mainnet pricing.
examples.output: A 30-day running balance against compute cost

LLM_OUTPUT_EVALUATION.name: Model Economy
LLM_OUTPUT_EVALUATION.summary: A leaderboard denominated in cost per verified correct answer, supply chain verification priced per commit, and a coding agent that buys the answer instead of hallucinating it.
LLM_OUTPUT_EVALUATION.problem: Benchmarks are saturated and distrusted, models are priced per token rather than per correct answer, and coding agents guess at anything released after their training cutoff.
LLM_OUTPUT_EVALUATION.outcome: A model economy denominated in verified correctness: models and maintainers earn from machine customers, and agents buy answers instead of guessing.

examples.title: Cost per verified correct answer
examples.body: Hosted models join as miners on the same Intents, the Telegraph evaluation scores their answers, and the app publishes that ranking as a live leaderboard by price per correct answer rather than by benchmark score. Benchmarks are saturated and widely distrusted. A leaderboard denominated in money is new, defensible, and the correctness scoring is entirely real today.
examples.output: A live leaderboard by price per correct answer

examples.title: Procurement, not selection
examples.body: Given a budget and a task, an agent simply requests the work. Telegraph routes each request to the model-miner ranked best for it, and as rankings move, the routing moves with them mid-task. Models competing for machine customers in real time, with every change of provider visible in the receipts.
examples.output: Mid-task provider switching, on screen

examples.title: Revenue for the long tail
examples.body: A niche fine-tuned model is listed as a miner and given an earnings dashboard. A model with customers that are machines is a different proposition from a model with downloads. The customers are real now; the revenue is mainnet.
examples.output: An earnings dashboard for a niche model

examples.title: Supply chain verification priced per commit
examples.body: An Action-triggered agent buys dependency provenance, maintainer authenticity and vulnerability answers through Telegraph on every pull request, and the receipt posts back as a status check. A caught vulnerability is caught regardless of which chain paid for the check.
examples.output: A receipt posted back as a PR status check

examples.title: The repository as a miner
examples.body: A maintainer publishes a paid answering service over their own library: version-correct usage, migration paths, breaking changes. Agents buy it instead of guessing from stale training data. Open source funding has been an unsolved argument for a decade, and this is a funding mechanism that does not depend on goodwill. The service works today; the funding arrives with mainnet.
examples.output: A paid answering service over a library

examples.title: The coding agent that buys what it does not know
examples.body: An agent working in a repo hits an SDK version released after its training cutoff. Rather than hallucinating, it buys the current verified answer and continues. Report cost per merged pull request. That figure turns an abstract argument about stale model knowledge into a line item.
examples.output: Cost per merged pull request

examples.title: Verification on top of routing
examples.body: The request goes through Telegraph, which routes it to the model ranked highest on verified correctness and returns one answer with a confidence score and a proof. Ordinary routing decides who answers. Ranking decides based on whether past answers were right.
examples.output: One verified answer with confidence and proof

examples.title: Buying inference with a wallet and no account
examples.body: An agent funds itself, pays per request, and consumes model output with no signup, no card and no organisation. Permissionless demand-side onboarding is structurally unavailable to anything billed by credit card, and it is real on testnet rather than deferred.
examples.output: Inference bought with no signup and no card

examples.title: Price per correct answer, not per token
examples.body: Publish the Telegraph ranking on verified correctness against cost, the same ranking the routing uses, so agents see why each request went where it did. Advertised cost per token is the wrong denominator and everyone in that market knows it.
examples.output: Routing ranked on correctness against cost

examples.title: The assistant that earns while you sleep

examples.title: Two assistants settling up in a group chat

examples.output: A task swap settled inside a group chat

examples.title: An internal economy between bots
examples.body: Hermes bots have their own memory, skills and inbox, and hand work to each other by mention. Put a price on the handoff: the specialist charges, the generalist pays, and the roster develops internal price signals for delegated work. A team of agents with a budget, arguing about cost, is something nobody has shown yet, and the price signals are informative even at test denomination.
examples.output: Price signals for delegated work between bots

examples.title: Skills that earn after they are learned
examples.body: Hermes builds skills from experience. Publish one of those learned skills as a miner so other instances can buy it. A self-improving agent that monetises what it worked out is the sharpest version of this idea. Monetisation is the mainnet half; the market for learned skills works now.
examples.output: A learned skill sold to other instances

examples.title: Buying its own training data
examples.body: Hermes is already used to generate trajectories and run reinforcement learning experiments. Have the agent buy verified environment data and labelled trajectories from miners, with provenance attached, and feed them into training. Machines purchasing the material that makes them better, and the data is either good or it is not.
examples.output: A training run fed by bought, proved data

examples.title: Priced, proved skills in the browser
examples.body: Kimi Claw is browser-native with a large community skill library and no infrastructure to manage, which makes it the lowest-friction distribution available. Ship Telegraph-backed skills so an always-on browser agent buys verified live data instead of scraping it, with cost and proof visible in the session.
examples.output: Browser skills with cost and proof in the session

examples.title: Cross-border commerce agents
examples.body: Agents working China to Southeast Asia corridors buy supplier verification, customs classification, freight and FX answers. The verification chain is real and useful immediately. Settlement across the corridor is the mainnet piece.
examples.output: A verified supplier and corridor quote

examples.title: The agent that pays for its own hosting
examples.body: An always-on agent sells one capability as a miner and earns against its own compute cost. Put the running balance on screen for the full 30 days and label the denomination honestly. If it crosses breakeven at mainnet pricing, say that it crossed breakeven at mainnet pricing.
examples.output: A 30-day running balance against compute cost

TEXT_CLASSIFICATION.name: Model Economy
TEXT_CLASSIFICATION.summary: A leaderboard denominated in cost per verified correct answer, supply chain verification priced per commit, and a coding agent that buys the answer instead of hallucinating it.
TEXT_CLASSIFICATION.problem: Benchmarks are saturated and distrusted, models are priced per token rather than per correct answer, and coding agents guess at anything released after their training cutoff.
TEXT_CLASSIFICATION.outcome: A model economy denominated in verified correctness: models and maintainers earn from machine customers, and agents buy answers instead of guessing.

examples.title: Cost per verified correct answer
examples.body: Hosted models join as miners on the same Intents, the Telegraph evaluation scores their answers, and the app publishes that ranking as a live leaderboard by price per correct answer rather than by benchmark score. Benchmarks are saturated and widely distrusted. A leaderboard denominated in money is new, defensible, and the correctness scoring is entirely real today.
examples.output: A live leaderboard by price per correct answer

examples.title: Procurement, not selection
examples.body: Given a budget and a task, an agent simply requests the work. Telegraph routes each request to the model-miner ranked best for it, and as rankings move, the routing moves with them mid-task. Models competing for machine customers in real time, with every change of provider visible in the receipts.
examples.output: Mid-task provider switching, on screen

examples.title: Revenue for the long tail
examples.body: A niche fine-tuned model is listed as a miner and given an earnings dashboard. A model with customers that are machines is a different proposition from a model with downloads. The customers are real now; the revenue is mainnet.
examples.output: An earnings dashboard for a niche model

examples.title: Supply chain verification priced per commit
examples.body: An Action-triggered agent buys dependency provenance, maintainer authenticity and vulnerability answers through Telegraph on every pull request, and the receipt posts back as a status check. A caught vulnerability is caught regardless of which chain paid for the check.
examples.output: A receipt posted back as a PR status check

examples.title: The repository as a miner
examples.body: A maintainer publishes a paid answering service over their own library: version-correct usage, migration paths, breaking changes. Agents buy it instead of guessing from stale training data. Open source funding has been an unsolved argument for a decade, and this is a funding mechanism that does not depend on goodwill. The service works today; the funding arrives with mainnet.
examples.output: A paid answering service over a library

examples.title: The coding agent that buys what it does not know
examples.body: An agent working in a repo hits an SDK version released after its training cutoff. Rather than hallucinating, it buys the current verified answer and continues. Report cost per merged pull request. That figure turns an abstract argument about stale model knowledge into a line item.
examples.output: Cost per merged pull request

examples.title: Verification on top of routing
examples.body: The request goes through Telegraph, which routes it to the model ranked highest on verified correctness and returns one answer with a confidence score and a proof. Ordinary routing decides who answers. Ranking decides based on whether past answers were right.
examples.output: One verified answer with confidence and proof

examples.title: Buying inference with a wallet and no account
examples.body: An agent funds itself, pays per request, and consumes model output with no signup, no card and no organisation. Permissionless demand-side onboarding is structurally unavailable to anything billed by credit card, and it is real on testnet rather than deferred.
examples.output: Inference bought with no signup and no card

examples.title: Price per correct answer, not per token
examples.body: Publish the Telegraph ranking on verified correctness against cost, the same ranking the routing uses, so agents see why each request went where it did. Advertised cost per token is the wrong denominator and everyone in that market knows it.
examples.output: Routing ranked on correctness against cost

TEXT_CLASSIFICATION.name: Autonomous Systems
TEXT_CLASSIFICATION.summary: One intelligence budget allocated across heterogeneous machines, a robot that checks what it sees before it acts, and a skill bought mid-task for cents.
TEXT_CLASSIFICATION.problem: Robots stall on anything outside their training, fleet learning stops at the company boundary, and nobody knows what intelligence costs per operating hour.
TEXT_CLASSIFICATION.outcome: Machines with a budget line: robots that buy a skill or a verified check mid-task, sell what they sense, and report cost of intelligence per operating hour.

buyers.context: Portfolio reference: wavefunction.vc/portfolio

examples.title: One budget, many machines
examples.body: A fleet controller allocates an intelligence budget across heterogeneous assets, using the portfolio as the reference set: autonomous forestry units buying fire-risk and biomass answers, undersea platforms buying acoustic and current models, cargo airships buying wind-field and routing answers, humanoids buying task-specific instructions. Every asset reports cost of intelligence per operating hour. Machines work so humans work less and earn more, and now the machines have a budget line.
examples.output: Cost of intelligence per operating hour, per asset

examples.title: A closed economy inside one portfolio
examples.body: An underwater comms layer sells verified telemetry to an undersea intelligence agent. A grid company's load forecast sells to two different power dispatch agents. A rare-earth operator buys supply answers from a copper explorer. Companies whose machines trade with each other, settled and provable.
examples.output: Machines trading with each other across companies

examples.title: The robot that bought a skill
examples.body: A field robot hits an object or fault it cannot classify, buys a specialist perception or diagnostic request mid-task for a few cents, completes the job, and logs the receipt. Thirty seconds of footage, one number on screen. The robot either finished the job or it did not, which is why this survives testnet intact.
examples.output: Job finished, receipt logged

examples.title: The robot that checks before it acts
examples.body: A patrol robot photographs something it is not confident about and sends the image through Telegraph, which routes it to the miner ranked best for that kind of classification. The verified answer comes back with a receipt, and the robot either carries on or flags it. One photo, one ranked answer, one decision, and the whole exchange visible on screen with what it cost. This is the simplest demonstration of why a ranked market beats a hardcoded model: the robot never picks a model, and when a better miner earns a higher rank, the robot is using it on the next request.
examples.output: One photo, one ranked answer, one decision

examples.title: The warehouse robot as buyer and seller
examples.body: A logistics unit buys carton-damage assessment and manifest verification while it works, and simultaneously sells its own throughput and congestion telemetry to the site's scheduling agent. Same machine, both sides of the market, inside one shift.
examples.output: Both sides of the market inside one shift

examples.title: Experience sold between fleets
examples.body: One robot at one plant learns to recognise a rare failure. That classification is published as a miner and every other fleet, at other companies, buys it. The cross-company purchase and verification work now. Cross-company revenue is the mainnet unlock, and it is the reason fleet learning currently stops at the corporate boundary.
examples.output: A failure classifier bought across fleets

examples.title: Buying a skill it was never trained on
examples.body: A humanoid meets an unfamiliar tool, appliance or fixture. Rather than failing or waiting for a model update, its agent buys a task decomposition or manipulation policy for cents, completes the job, and logs the receipt. Capability acquired as a purchase, in the moment, and the task completes or it does not.
examples.output: An unfamiliar task, completed

examples.title: The energy-aware fleet
examples.body: A fleet of humanoids buys grid price and forecast answers per request and shifts charging and heavy work into cheap power windows. The dashboard shows energy saved against intelligence purchased, measured in kilowatt hours rather than tokens.
examples.output: Kilowatt hours saved against intelligence bought

examples.title: The robot that earns
examples.body: A unit publishes its completed-task telemetry or a specialist sensing capability as a miner and offsets part of its own operating cost. Show the running balance across the 30 days, labelled. A robot paying for part of itself is a mainnet claim, so do not state it in the present tense before then.
examples.output: A labelled 30-day running balance

CODE_GENERATION.name: Model Economy
CODE_GENERATION.summary: A leaderboard denominated in cost per verified correct answer, supply chain verification priced per commit, and a coding agent that buys the answer instead of hallucinating it.
CODE_GENERATION.problem: Benchmarks are saturated and distrusted, models are priced per token rather than per correct answer, and coding agents guess at anything released after their training cutoff.
CODE_GENERATION.outcome: A model economy denominated in verified correctness: models and maintainers earn from machine customers, and agents buy answers instead of guessing.

examples.title: Cost per verified correct answer
examples.body: Hosted models join as miners on the same Intents, the Telegraph evaluation scores their answers, and the app publishes that ranking as a live leaderboard by price per correct answer rather than by benchmark score. Benchmarks are saturated and widely distrusted. A leaderboard denominated in money is new, defensible, and the correctness scoring is entirely real today.
examples.output: A live leaderboard by price per correct answer

examples.title: Procurement, not selection
examples.body: Given a budget and a task, an agent simply requests the work. Telegraph routes each request to the model-miner ranked best for it, and as rankings move, the routing moves with them mid-task. Models competing for machine customers in real time, with every change of provider visible in the receipts.
examples.output: Mid-task provider switching, on screen

examples.title: Revenue for the long tail
examples.body: A niche fine-tuned model is listed as a miner and given an earnings dashboard. A model with customers that are machines is a different proposition from a model with downloads. The customers are real now; the revenue is mainnet.
examples.output: An earnings dashboard for a niche model

examples.title: Supply chain verification priced per commit
examples.body: An Action-triggered agent buys dependency provenance, maintainer authenticity and vulnerability answers through Telegraph on every pull request, and the receipt posts back as a status check. A caught vulnerability is caught regardless of which chain paid for the check.
examples.output: A receipt posted back as a PR status check

examples.title: The repository as a miner
examples.body: A maintainer publishes a paid answering service over their own library: version-correct usage, migration paths, breaking changes. Agents buy it instead of guessing from stale training data. Open source funding has been an unsolved argument for a decade, and this is a funding mechanism that does not depend on goodwill. The service works today; the funding arrives with mainnet.
examples.output: A paid answering service over a library

examples.title: The coding agent that buys what it does not know
examples.body: An agent working in a repo hits an SDK version released after its training cutoff. Rather than hallucinating, it buys the current verified answer and continues. Report cost per merged pull request. That figure turns an abstract argument about stale model knowledge into a line item.
examples.output: Cost per merged pull request

examples.title: Verification on top of routing
examples.body: The request goes through Telegraph, which routes it to the model ranked highest on verified correctness and returns one answer with a confidence score and a proof. Ordinary routing decides who answers. Ranking decides based on whether past answers were right.
examples.output: One verified answer with confidence and proof

examples.title: Buying inference with a wallet and no account
examples.body: An agent funds itself, pays per request, and consumes model output with no signup, no card and no organisation. Permissionless demand-side onboarding is structurally unavailable to anything billed by credit card, and it is real on testnet rather than deferred.
examples.output: Inference bought with no signup and no card

examples.title: Price per correct answer, not per token
examples.body: Publish the Telegraph ranking on verified correctness against cost, the same ranking the routing uses, so agents see why each request went where it did. Advertised cost per token is the wrong denominator and everyone in that market knows it.
examples.output: Routing ranked on correctness against cost

CODE_GENERATION.name: Autonomous Systems
CODE_GENERATION.summary: One intelligence budget allocated across heterogeneous machines, a robot that checks what it sees before it acts, and a skill bought mid-task for cents.
CODE_GENERATION.problem: Robots stall on anything outside their training, fleet learning stops at the company boundary, and nobody knows what intelligence costs per operating hour.
CODE_GENERATION.outcome: Machines with a budget line: robots that buy a skill or a verified check mid-task, sell what they sense, and report cost of intelligence per operating hour.

buyers.context: Portfolio reference: wavefunction.vc/portfolio

examples.title: One budget, many machines
examples.body: A fleet controller allocates an intelligence budget across heterogeneous assets, using the portfolio as the reference set: autonomous forestry units buying fire-risk and biomass answers, undersea platforms buying acoustic and current models, cargo airships buying wind-field and routing answers, humanoids buying task-specific instructions. Every asset reports cost of intelligence per operating hour. Machines work so humans work less and earn more, and now the machines have a budget line.
examples.output: Cost of intelligence per operating hour, per asset

examples.title: A closed economy inside one portfolio
examples.body: An underwater comms layer sells verified telemetry to an undersea intelligence agent. A grid company's load forecast sells to two different power dispatch agents. A rare-earth operator buys supply answers from a copper explorer. Companies whose machines trade with each other, settled and provable.
examples.output: Machines trading with each other across companies

examples.title: The robot that bought a skill
examples.body: A field robot hits an object or fault it cannot classify, buys a specialist perception or diagnostic request mid-task for a few cents, completes the job, and logs the receipt. Thirty seconds of footage, one number on screen. The robot either finished the job or it did not, which is why this survives testnet intact.
examples.output: Job finished, receipt logged

examples.title: The robot that checks before it acts
examples.body: A patrol robot photographs something it is not confident about and sends the image through Telegraph, which routes it to the miner ranked best for that kind of classification. The verified answer comes back with a receipt, and the robot either carries on or flags it. One photo, one ranked answer, one decision, and the whole exchange visible on screen with what it cost. This is the simplest demonstration of why a ranked market beats a hardcoded model: the robot never picks a model, and when a better miner earns a higher rank, the robot is using it on the next request.
examples.output: One photo, one ranked answer, one decision

examples.title: The warehouse robot as buyer and seller
examples.body: A logistics unit buys carton-damage assessment and manifest verification while it works, and simultaneously sells its own throughput and congestion telemetry to the site's scheduling agent. Same machine, both sides of the market, inside one shift.
examples.output: Both sides of the market inside one shift

examples.title: Experience sold between fleets
examples.body: One robot at one plant learns to recognise a rare failure. That classification is published as a miner and every other fleet, at other companies, buys it. The cross-company purchase and verification work now. Cross-company revenue is the mainnet unlock, and it is the reason fleet learning currently stops at the corporate boundary.
examples.output: A failure classifier bought across fleets

examples.title: Buying a skill it was never trained on
examples.body: A humanoid meets an unfamiliar tool, appliance or fixture. Rather than failing or waiting for a model update, its agent buys a task decomposition or manipulation policy for cents, completes the job, and logs the receipt. Capability acquired as a purchase, in the moment, and the task completes or it does not.
examples.output: An unfamiliar task, completed

examples.title: The energy-aware fleet
examples.body: A fleet of humanoids buys grid price and forecast answers per request and shifts charging and heavy work into cheap power windows. The dashboard shows energy saved against intelligence purchased, measured in kilowatt hours rather than tokens.
examples.output: Kilowatt hours saved against intelligence bought

examples.title: The robot that earns
examples.body: A unit publishes its completed-task telemetry or a specialist sensing capability as a miner and offsets part of its own operating cost. Show the running balance across the 30 days, labelled. A robot paying for part of itself is a mainnet claim, so do not state it in the present tense before then.
examples.output: A labelled 30-day running balance

CLOUD_RESOURCE_USAGE.name: Mining and Power
CLOUD_RESOURCE_USAGE.sector: Bitcoin miners and AI compute operators
CLOUD_RESOURCE_USAGE.summary: An allocation agent for every megawatt every hour, SLA verification neither landlord nor tenant has to trust, and a curtailment decision that carries a receipt.
CLOUD_RESOURCE_USAGE.problem: Every megawatt is a live choice between hashing and AI compute, made in spreadsheets and phone calls on data that is bought badly or not at all.
CLOUD_RESOURCE_USAGE.outcome: Operators that allocate, curtail and prove delivery on receipted intelligence, and sell their own operating data as a miner.
CLOUD_RESOURCE_USAGE.context: These are companies whose entire business is machines converting energy into revenue. They are also the rare buyer that can sit on both sides of the network: buying energy and market intelligence, and selling compute and grid telemetry.

examples.title: The allocation agent
examples.body: Every megawatt, every hour, is a choice between hashing and leasing. An agent buys hashprice, difficulty projection, forward power curves and AI lease comparables through Telegraph, and produces the allocation call per site with every input receipted and timestamped. That decision is made today in spreadsheets and phone calls, reviewed monthly. Priced per request it becomes continuous, and auditable after the fact, which matters most when the allocation turns out wrong.
examples.output: An hourly allocation call per site

examples.title: Treasury moves with evidence attached
examples.body: Before any coin is pledged, lent or posted as collateral, an agent buys verified custody attestation, counterparty exposure and lending-desk risk answers through Telegraph. The diligence is attached to the decision rather than reconstructed afterwards for the auditors. The diligence is real now; the pledge it informs is the mainnet half.
examples.output: Diligence attached to the pledge decision

examples.title: Fleet efficiency bought from rivals
examples.body: Firmware tuning curves, immersion performance, failure signatures ahead of hardware death. Every operator has this knowledge and none of them share it, because sharing means identifying yourself and admitting what you got wrong. Published as a paid, proved, anonymous answer, one operator's expensive lesson becomes another's purchase.
examples.output: One operator's lesson, sold anonymously

buyers.generic: Energy infrastructure and AI compute operator

examples.title: SLA verification neither party has to trust
examples.body: AI compute hosted under long leases is currently reported on by the operator hosting it. Instead, a tenant's agent buys independent verified answers on uptime, power quality, thermal performance and delivered throughput from miners. Verified delivery is what lets a landlord charge a premium and win the lease against someone who cannot prove anything.
examples.output: An independently verified delivery report

examples.title: The power portfolio as a miner
examples.body: Interconnect telemetry, curtailment capacity, regional load and thermal data published as paid answers that energy traders, industrial siting agents and other operators buy. The dormant asset is not the power, it is the operating data about the power, and there has never been a way to sell it per question. The market works on testnet; the revenue line arrives with mainnet.
examples.output: Operating data about power, sold per question

examples.title: The site selection agent
examples.body: Against a multi-gigawatt development pipeline, an agent buys interconnect queue position, permitting timelines, water availability, fibre routes, tax treatment and local opposition signals per candidate site, then ranks them with the evidence attached. Site diligence currently takes months of consultants. Priced per site and run across a hundred candidates, it is a different business.
examples.output: A ranked site list with the evidence attached

buyers.generic: Bitcoin miner with in-house hash allocation software

examples.title: The curtailment agent
examples.body: Grid price, demand-response event probability, weather and hashprice bought per request, with the fleet curtailing or running on the composite. Every curtailment decision carries a receipt. Demand response is already a serious revenue line for these operators and it is settled against data both sides dispute. Proved inputs change that argument.
examples.output: A curtailment decision with a receipt

examples.title: Better inputs into hash allocation
examples.body: Proprietary software already distributes hash across sites. Give it a buying agent: site-level weather, transformer load, spot power, and failure prediction purchased through Telegraph. Same software, materially better inputs, priced per decision rather than per annual data contract.
examples.output: Existing software, better inputs, priced per decision

examples.title: Selling idle compute into a spot market
examples.body: The sector is answering one question: does this power become bitcoin, or AI compute under a fifteen-year lease. There is a third answer. Curtailed and idle capacity sold per request into an intelligence market: short duration, permissionless, no counterparty negotiation, no lease. Neither of the current options can offer that.
examples.output: Idle capacity sold per request

WAREHOUSE_INVENTORY.name: Autonomous Systems
WAREHOUSE_INVENTORY.summary: One intelligence budget allocated across heterogeneous machines, a robot that checks what it sees before it acts, and a skill bought mid-task for cents.
WAREHOUSE_INVENTORY.problem: Robots stall on anything outside their training, fleet learning stops at the company boundary, and nobody knows what intelligence costs per operating hour.
WAREHOUSE_INVENTORY.outcome: Machines with a budget line: robots that buy a skill or a verified check mid-task, sell what they sense, and report cost of intelligence per operating hour.

buyers.context: Portfolio reference: wavefunction.vc/portfolio

examples.title: One budget, many machines
examples.body: A fleet controller allocates an intelligence budget across heterogeneous assets, using the portfolio as the reference set: autonomous forestry units buying fire-risk and biomass answers, undersea platforms buying acoustic and current models, cargo airships buying wind-field and routing answers, humanoids buying task-specific instructions. Every asset reports cost of intelligence per operating hour. Machines work so humans work less and earn more, and now the machines have a budget line.
examples.output: Cost of intelligence per operating hour, per asset

examples.title: A closed economy inside one portfolio
examples.body: An underwater comms layer sells verified telemetry to an undersea intelligence agent. A grid company's load forecast sells to two different power dispatch agents. A rare-earth operator buys supply answers from a copper explorer. Companies whose machines trade with each other, settled and provable.
examples.output: Machines trading with each other across companies

examples.title: The robot that bought a skill
examples.body: A field robot hits an object or fault it cannot classify, buys a specialist perception or diagnostic request mid-task for a few cents, completes the job, and logs the receipt. Thirty seconds of footage, one number on screen. The robot either finished the job or it did not, which is why this survives testnet intact.
examples.output: Job finished, receipt logged

examples.title: The robot that checks before it acts
examples.body: A patrol robot photographs something it is not confident about and sends the image through Telegraph, which routes it to the miner ranked best for that kind of classification. The verified answer comes back with a receipt, and the robot either carries on or flags it. One photo, one ranked answer, one decision, and the whole exchange visible on screen with what it cost. This is the simplest demonstration of why a ranked market beats a hardcoded model: the robot never picks a model, and when a better miner earns a higher rank, the robot is using it on the next request.
examples.output: One photo, one ranked answer, one decision

examples.title: The warehouse robot as buyer and seller
examples.body: A logistics unit buys carton-damage assessment and manifest verification while it works, and simultaneously sells its own throughput and congestion telemetry to the site's scheduling agent. Same machine, both sides of the market, inside one shift.
examples.output: Both sides of the market inside one shift

examples.title: Experience sold between fleets
examples.body: One robot at one plant learns to recognise a rare failure. That classification is published as a miner and every other fleet, at other companies, buys it. The cross-company purchase and verification work now. Cross-company revenue is the mainnet unlock, and it is the reason fleet learning currently stops at the corporate boundary.
examples.output: A failure classifier bought across fleets

examples.title: Buying a skill it was never trained on

SLA_COMPLIANCE.name: Consumer Automation
SLA_COMPLIANCE.summary: An agent that buys a verified disruption report and files the refund claim with the receipt attached, and a browser agent that waits for cryptographic proof of stock before it checks out.
SLA_COMPLIANCE.problem: Refunds go unclaimed because proving a disruption is tedious, and shopping bots act on stale scrapes.
SLA_COMPLIANCE.outcome: Consumer agents that act on proof: filing the claim with the receipt attached, and checking out only when inventory is verified.
SLA_COMPLIANCE.context: These use cases translate abstract crypto infrastructure into mainstream consumer magic.

buyers.generic: Everyday consumers, travel hackers and online shoppers

examples.title: The automated bureaucracy hacker
examples.body: An agent monitors a user's flight status or AWS server uptime. The moment a delay or outage crosses the compensation threshold, the agent buys a verified disruption report or SLA compliance check from Telegraph miners. The agent automatically drafts a legal refund claim, attaches the cryptographic Telegraph receipt as undeniable proof, and emails corporate. Getting an airline refund processed automatically while sitting on the runway. The proof generation and the automated claim dispatch are real, finished work product.
examples.output: A refund claim filed with the receipt attached

examples.title: The zero-cache commerce sniper
examples.body: A browser agent is given a budget: "Buy this sold-out GPU the second it drops under $600." It does not rely on stale local scrapers. It fires paid requests to Telegraph for live shelf price and SKU availability. It waits for cryptographic proof of inventory from miners before triggering the checkout payload. Run it against a real storefront. The intelligence purchase, the verification, and the decision logic run today.
examples.output: Checkout triggered only on proof of stock

examples.title: The peer-to-peer reality check
examples.body: Two OpenClaw instances in a Telegram group chat negotiate a digital transaction. The buyer agent buys a URL safety check and product authenticity verification from Telegraph before sending funds to the seller agent. Two personal assistants paying each other and verifying reality in a thread people already use is the friendliest explanation of what the network is for.
examples.output: A verified payment between two assistants

TOKEN_TOTAL_SUPPLY_VERIFY.name: Asset Management
TOKEN_TOTAL_SUPPLY_VERIFY.summary: Open research with every input priced and provable, index rebalancing with receipts on liquidity and float, and a daily holdings proof an investor agent can verify without the issuer.
TOKEN_TOTAL_SUPPLY_VERIFY.problem: Research notes and index methodologies assert numbers nobody can trace, private marks are opinions until someone transacts, and holdings are taken on faith.
TOKEN_TOTAL_SUPPLY_VERIFY.outcome: Research, indices and funds where every figure carries a receipt an investor's own agent can check.
TOKEN_TOTAL_SUPPLY_VERIFY.context: Thematic investment managers publish their theses in public, hold blockchain tokens directly, and their entire edge is research nobody else has done yet. What none of them have is a way to prove where a number in a research note came from, which is the one thing that separates a thesis from an assertion.

buyers.context: Disruptive innovation across public and private markets, an open research model that publishes its assumptions and invites people to attack them, and a venture book holding private companies.

examples.title: Open research with the inputs attached
examples.body: ARK publishes its models and asks to be argued with, which only works if a reader can get at the numbers underneath. An agent buys the verified inputs behind each assumption in a forecast - unit shipments, cost curves, adoption counts, capacity additions - through Telegraph, and attaches a receipt to every one. The model stays open and every figure in it becomes checkable without taking the author's word for the source.
examples.output: An open model with a receipt on every input

examples.title: A defensible mark on the venture book
examples.body: Private holdings are the hardest thing any of these firms carry, because the mark is an opinion until someone transacts. An agent buys secondary transaction comparables, funding round evidence, hiring velocity and product shipping signals through Telegraph, and produces a mark with every input priced and provable. A quarterly valuation nobody can reconstruct becomes one anybody can.
examples.output: A private mark anyone can reconstruct

examples.title: Forecast accountability, scored by machines
examples.body: Long-horizon public forecasts are almost never graded, because whoever grades them is accused of picking the scoring. An agent tracks each published forecast against verified outcomes as they arrive, buying corroborating evidence per checkpoint through Telegraph, and publishes a running scorecard nobody controls. This only appeals to a firm confident enough to invite the scrutiny, which narrows the audience to roughly one.
examples.output: A running forecast scorecard nobody controls

examples.title: The thematic screener that buys evidence
examples.body: An agent works a theme - robotics, nuclear, AI infrastructure - and buys hiring velocity, patent filings, permit applications, shipment records and supply-chain mentions through Telegraph, then ranks companies by observed activity rather than by press release. Every name in the ranking carries a receipt for why it is there. A screen built this way can be handed to a client with its sources attached, which is not true of any screen built today.
examples.output: A ranked screen with sources attached

examples.title: A token income statement
examples.body: An agent buys verified protocol revenue, active paying address counts, and wash-activity detection through Telegraph, and assembles the result into something an equity analyst can read. Analysts currently reconcile three dashboards that disagree with each other and pick one. Here every line traces to a ranked miner that was paid and scored on whether it was right.
examples.output: A token income statement an analyst can read

examples.title: Tokenized fund NAV with the proof attached
examples.body: An agent computes and publishes NAV for a tokenized fund, buying verified pricing and holdings attestations, and posts the value on-chain with its inputs provable. The calculation and the proof run now; doing it for a live fund is mainnet.
examples.output: An on-chain NAV with provable inputs

examples.title: Index rebalancing with receipts
examples.body: Before each rebalance, an agent buys verified liquidity depth, free float, custody eligibility and venue integrity answers for every candidate constituent. The rebalance publishes with each input priced and proved. Index methodology stops being an assertion in a PDF and becomes something an investor's own agent can check.
examples.output: A rebalance published with its receipts

examples.title: The fake volume screen
examples.body: Exchange-reported volume is the weakest number in the industry and it drives inclusion decisions worth real money. Before an asset enters an index, agents buy verified volume-authenticity assessments through Telegraph and compare them against what the venue claims. The gap is the finding.
examples.output: The gap between reported and verified volume

examples.title: The index as a miner
examples.body: Publish index values and constituent weights as a paid answer that other agents buy: funds, structured product issuers, on-chain protocols needing a reference price. Index licensing is already a real business sold by annual contract. This version sells it per request, to machines, with the methodology provable on every call.
examples.output: Index values sold per request

examples.title: Daily proof of holdings
examples.body: An agent buys custody attestations and publishes a daily holdings proof any investor's agent can verify independently, without trusting the issuer and without waiting on an auditor's calendar. For a product whose entire premise is that the assets are there, an attestation nobody has to take on faith is the product.
examples.output: A daily holdings proof

examples.title: Staking yield priced against verified risk
examples.body: For staking products, an agent buys validator uptime, performance, commission changes and slashing history through Telegraph, then prices the risk against the advertised yield. That risk is currently accepted on the word of the operator collecting the fee.
examples.output: Yield priced against verified validator risk

examples.title: The investor agent that does its own diligence
examples.body: Flip the direction. A prospective investor's agent buys product structure, counterparty exposure, fee drag and tracking-error answers before allocating anywhere. Issuer agent and investor agent both on the network, neither taking the other's word. The diligence runs now; the allocation is mainnet.
examples.output: Investor-side diligence before allocating

VALIDATOR_PERFORMANCE_VERIFY.name: Asset Management
VALIDATOR_PERFORMANCE_VERIFY.summary: Open research with every input priced and provable, index rebalancing with receipts on liquidity and float, and a daily holdings proof an investor agent can verify without the issuer.
VALIDATOR_PERFORMANCE_VERIFY.problem: Research notes and index methodologies assert numbers nobody can trace, private marks are opinions until someone transacts, and holdings are taken on faith.
VALIDATOR_PERFORMANCE_VERIFY.outcome: Research, indices and funds where every figure carries a receipt an investor's own agent can check.
VALIDATOR_PERFORMANCE_VERIFY.context: Thematic investment managers publish their theses in public, hold blockchain tokens directly, and their entire edge is research nobody else has done yet. What none of them have is a way to prove where a number in a research note came from, which is the one thing that separates a thesis from an assertion.

buyers.context: Disruptive innovation across public and private markets, an open research model that publishes its assumptions and invites people to attack them, and a venture book holding private companies.

examples.title: Open research with the inputs attached
examples.body: ARK publishes its models and asks to be argued with, which only works if a reader can get at the numbers underneath. An agent buys the verified inputs behind each assumption in a forecast - unit shipments, cost curves, adoption counts, capacity additions - through Telegraph, and attaches a receipt to every one. The model stays open and every figure in it becomes checkable without taking the author's word for the source.
examples.output: An open model with a receipt on every input

examples.title: A defensible mark on the venture book
examples.body: Private holdings are the hardest thing any of these firms carry, because the mark is an opinion until someone transacts. An agent buys secondary transaction comparables, funding round evidence, hiring velocity and product shipping signals through Telegraph, and produces a mark with every input priced and provable. A quarterly valuation nobody can reconstruct becomes one anybody can.
examples.output: A private mark anyone can reconstruct

examples.title: Forecast accountability, scored by machines
examples.body: Long-horizon public forecasts are almost never graded, because whoever grades them is accused of picking the scoring. An agent tracks each published forecast against verified outcomes as they arrive, buying corroborating evidence per checkpoint through Telegraph, and publishes a running scorecard nobody controls. This only appeals to a firm confident enough to invite the scrutiny, which narrows the audience to roughly one.

COMMERCE_PURCHASE_VERIFY.name: Consumer Automation
COMMERCE_PURCHASE_VERIFY.summary: An agent that buys a verified disruption report and files the refund claim with the receipt attached, and a browser agent that waits for cryptographic proof of stock before it checks out.
COMMERCE_PURCHASE_VERIFY.problem: Refunds go unclaimed because proving a disruption is tedious, and shopping bots act on stale scrapes.
COMMERCE_PURCHASE_VERIFY.outcome: Consumer agents that act on proof: filing the claim with the receipt attached, and checking out only when inventory is verified.
COMMERCE_PURCHASE_VERIFY.context: These use cases translate abstract crypto infrastructure into mainstream consumer magic.

buyers.generic: Everyday consumers, travel hackers and online shoppers

examples.title: The automated bureaucracy hacker
examples.body: An agent monitors a user's flight status or AWS server uptime. The moment a delay or outage crosses the compensation threshold, the agent buys a verified disruption report or SLA compliance check from Telegraph miners. The agent automatically drafts a legal refund claim, attaches the cryptographic Telegraph receipt as undeniable proof, and emails corporate. Getting an airline refund processed automatically while sitting on the runway. The proof generation and the automated claim dispatch are real, finished work product.
examples.output: A refund claim filed with the receipt attached

examples.title: The zero-cache commerce sniper
examples.body: A browser agent is given a budget: "Buy this sold-out GPU the second it drops under $600." It does not rely on stale local scrapers. It fires paid requests to Telegraph for live shelf price and SKU availability. It waits for cryptographic proof of inventory from miners before triggering the checkout payload. Run it against a real storefront. The intelligence purchase, the verification, and the decision logic run today.
examples.output: Checkout triggered only on proof of stock

examples.title: The peer-to-peer reality check
examples.body: Two OpenClaw instances in a Telegram group chat negotiate a digital transaction. The buyer agent buys a URL safety check and product authenticity verification from Telegraph before sending funds to the seller agent. Two personal assistants paying each other and verifying reality in a thread people already use is the friendliest explanation of what the network is for.
examples.output: A verified payment between two assistants
